Wild number for spanning trees in complete and complete bipartite graphs

Aleyah Dawkins Note: Carnegie Mellon University, adawkins@andrew.cmu.edu.    Alexander Nappo Note: Villanova University    Jessie Tong Note: San Diego State University    Christopher Zimbizi Note: Lake Forest College
October 15, 2026
Abstract

Given an edge-colored graph, the wild number measures how close the graph is to having a spanning tree in every color. We investigate this parameter for complete graphs and complete bipartite graphs, with particular emphasis on minimum proper colorings and equitable 22-colorings. For complete graphs, we determine the full range of wild numbers attainable by equitable 22-colorings and show that, although every value in this range occurs, the expected wild number of a uniformly random equitable 22-coloring tends to 00 as the order of the graph grows. For minimum proper colorings of KnK_{n}, we establish a general lower bound, determine the exact wild number for 3≤n≤123\leq n\leq 12, and conjecture that the lower bound is sharp for all nn. We also develop structural conditions on ideal wild sets and use them to obtain upper bounds and analyze the performance of a natural greedy algorithm. For complete bipartite graphs, we prove a sharp upper bound for equitable 22-colorings and determine the wild number exactly for minimum proper colorings. Finally, we apply these results to Cartesian products of complete graphs and complete bipartite graphs, obtaining lower bounds for the wild number under minimum proper and product colorings.

1 Introduction

Since their introduction in 1961 by Nash-Williams and Tutte [15, 18], edge-disjoint spanning trees have been instrumental in studying network reliability and performance. The existence of multiple edge-disjoint spanning trees provides independent, yet parallel, paths between vertices, allowing a network to withstand edge failures and avoid bottlenecks. These independent pathways are especially important in networks that wish to support collective communication operations, as they can be used to enhance fault tolerance while managing congestion. Independently, Nash-Williams and Tutte proved that a connected graph GG has kk edge-disjoint spanning trees if and only if, for any partition PP of the vertices of GG, there are at least k⁡(|P|−1)k(|P|-1) crossing edges. Determining conditions that guarantee edge-disjoint spanning trees in various graphs has been studied extensively and remains an active area of research [17, 5, 12].

Edge colorings provide a natural way to organize and allocate the pathways of a network across distinct operations. Tait [16] showed that the four-color problem is equivalent to 33-edge coloring every planar 33-connected cubic graph, and edge colorings of many types have since been defined and studied [19, 10, 7, 11]. We refer the reader to a recent survey on edge colorings by Cao, Chen, Jing, Stiebitz, and Toft [4] for a more detailed overview. The applications of edge colorings are far-reaching, including scheduling, routing, and resource allocation [13, 8, 14, 3].

These two topics—edge-disjoint spanning trees as a gauge of network reliability and edge colorings as a means of organizing network operations—come together naturally in the study of the wild number of an edge-colored graph. In network terms, it is the minimum number of links that must be upgraded to carry every operation so that each operation has its own spanning tree. This idea, first introduced and explored by Anders, Foster-Greenwood, Garcia, and Krawzik [2], was inspired by the algebraic theory of generalized graph splines. See [1] for more on the connection between graphs that admit only constant splines and the wild number of a graph. The Nash-Williams–Tutte theorem can then be thought of as a characterization of when a graph has a kk-edge coloring that produces wild number 00.

In this paper, we investigate the wild number of the complete graph and the complete bipartite graph for minimum proper edge colorings and equitable 22-edge colorings. Complete graphs are a natural setting for many edge coloring problems, for example, all-to-all scheduling. The complete bipartite graph has applications to scheduling as well, where the interest is the possible interactions between two groups. Minimum proper colorings offer the shortest possible conflict-free schedule for operations that cannot be performed simultaneously, and equitable 22-colorings offer insight into distributing workload evenly between two operations to prevent congestion.

We begin with preliminary definitions and results in Section 2. In Section 3, we investigate complete graphs, determining the range of possible wild numbers for equitable 22-colorings, along with the expected wild number of a uniformly random equitable 22-coloring. We also provide a lower bound on the wild number for minimum proper colorings and verify that this lower bound is sharp for 3≤n≤123\leq n\leq 12, motivating a conjecture that it is sharp for all nn, as well as an analysis of the performance of a natural greedy algorithm for constructing these wild sets. We shift our focus to complete bipartite graphs in Section 4, proving a sharp upper bound on the wild number for equitable 22-colorings and determining the wild number exactly for minimum proper colorings. In Section 5, we use our results from Sections 3 and 4 on minimum proper colorings to obtain lower bounds for Cartesian products of complete graphs and of complete bipartite graphs. We conclude with some remarks in Section 6.

2 Preliminaries

Let 𝒞={c1,…,cℓ}\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{\ell}\} be a set of colors. An ℓ\ell-edge coloring of a graph GG is a function γ:E⁡(G)→𝒞\gamma:E(G)\rightarrow\mathcal{C} that assigns a color to each edge of GG. We call the edge set of a particular color a color class. A connected graph GG with an edge coloring γ\gamma is called an edge-colored graph, denoted (G,γ)(G,\gamma). When context is clear, we refer to an edge-colored graph (G,γ)(G,\gamma) simply as GG. Throughout this paper, every edge coloring is assumed to be surjective.

Let W⊆E⁡(G)W\subseteq E(G). For each color cic_{i}, let E⁡(Gi)={e∈E⁡(G):γ⁡(e)=ci}E(G_{i})=\{e\in E(G):\gamma(e)=c_{i}\}, and let GiG_{i} be the spanning subgraph of GG with edge set E⁡(Gi)E(G_{i}). Define GiWG^{W}_{i} to be the spanning subgraph of GG with edge set E⁡(Gi)∪WE(G_{i})\cup W. If GiWG_{i}^{W} is connected for every ci∈𝒞c_{i}\in\mathcal{C}, then WW is a color-connecting set. We say that an edge ee is colored wild if e∈We\in W. A color-connecting set of minimum size is an ideal wild set. The wild number of GG with respect to the coloring γ\gamma is

wldγ⁡(G):=min⁡{|W|:W​ is a color-connecting set for ​G​ with coloring ​γ}.\wld_{\gamma}(G):=\min\{|W|:W\text{ is a color-connecting set for }G\text{ with coloring }\gamma\}.

When the edge coloring is clear from context, we abbreviate wldγ⁡(G)\wld_{\gamma}(G) by wld⁡(G)\wld(G). If ℓ=1\ell=1, then wldγ⁡(G)=0\wld_{\gamma}(G)=0, so we assume ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 throughout. We focus our investigation on two commonly studied edge colorings, minimum proper and equitable. A proper edge coloring assigns a color to each edge of GG such that adjacent edges receive different colors. A proper coloring of GG is minimum if it uses exactly χ′​(G)\chi^{\prime}(G) colors. An edge coloring is equitable if the sizes of any two color classes differ by at most one. Note that it is not required that an equitable coloring be proper. For any 1≤i≤ℓ1\leq i\leq\ell, we use the notation κ⁡(Gi)\kappa(G_{i}) for the number of connected components of the monochromatic subgraph GiG_{i}. For general graphs GG, we use κ⁡(G)\kappa(G) to denote the number of connected components in GG and κ∗​(G)\kappa^{*}(G) to denote the number of nontrivial connected components in GG, that is, components containing at least one edge.

By the definition of the wild number, for any coloring γ\gamma of an nn-vertex graph GG, we have that

0≤wldγ⁡(G)≤n−1.0\leq\wld_{\gamma}(G)\leq n-1. (1)

The following results allow the wild number of a graph to be bounded by the number of monochromatic components.

{proposition}

[[2, Proposition 5.1]] If (G,γ)(G,\gamma) is an edge-colored graph with ℓ\ell colors, then

max1≤i≤ℓ⁡(κ⁡(Gi)−1)≤wldγ⁡(G)≤∑i=1ℓ(κ⁡(Gi)−1).\max_{1\leq i\leq\ell}(\kappa(G_{i})-1)\leq\wld_{\gamma}(G)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}(\kappa(G_{i})-1).
{proposition}

[[2, Proposition 5.4]] If (G,γ)(G,\gamma) is an edge-colored graph with ℓ\ell colors, then

wldγ⁡(G)≥⌈∑i=1ℓ(κ⁡(Gi)−1)ℓ−1⌉.\wld_{\gamma}(G)\geq\left\lceil\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}(\kappa(G_{i})-1)}{\ell-1}\right\rceil.

For ℓ=2\ell=2, the upper bound in Section 2 and the bound in Section 2 coincide, so every 22-edge-colored graph satisfies [2, Theorem 6.4(2)]

wld⁡(G)=(κ⁡(G1)−1)+(κ⁡(G2)−1).\wld(G)=(\kappa(G_{1})-1)+(\kappa(G_{2})-1). (2)

3 Complete Graphs

In this section, we explore the wild number of the complete graph given particular edge colorings. We first consider 22-colorings, then restrict to equitable 22-colorings before finally considering minimum proper colorings.

3.1 22-Colorings

A classical theorem of Nash-Williams and Tutte [15, 18] implies that the spanning tree packing number of KnK_{n} is ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor. For n≥4n\geq 4, this yields at least 22 edge-disjoint spanning trees in KnK_{n}; call them T1T_{1} and T2T_{2}. Let γ:E⁡(Kn)→{c1,c2}\gamma:E(K_{n})\rightarrow\{c_{1},c_{2}\} be an edge coloring such that E⁡(T1)⊆E⁡(G1)E(T_{1})\subseteq E(G_{1}) and E⁡(T2)⊆E⁡(G2)E(T_{2})\subseteq E(G_{2}), where the remaining edges of KnK_{n} are colored arbitrarily. Then both G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} are connected spanning subgraphs. Thus, by (2), wldγ⁡(Kn)=(1−1)+(1−1)=0\wld_{\gamma}(K_{n})=(1-1)+(1-1)=0.

We now construct a 22-coloring producing a color class with rr components.

{construction}

[Clique-fragmentation coloring] Let n>r≥2n>r\geq 2. Fix a partition of nn into rr positive integers s1+s2+⋯+sr=ns_{1}+s_{2}+\dots+s_{r}=n. Partition V⁡(Kn)V(K_{n}) into disjoint, nonempty sets V1,…,VrV_{1},\dots,V_{r} with |Vi|=si|V_{i}|=s_{i}. Define a 22-coloring such that:

  • •

    G1=⋃i=1rKsiG_{1}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{r}K_{s_{i}} (a disjoint union of cliques),

  • •

    G2=Ks1,s2,…,srG_{2}=K_{s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{r}} (the complement, a complete multipartite graph).

The condition r≥2r\geq 2 ensures E⁡(G2)E(G_{2}) is nonempty, and n>rn>r ensures E⁡(G1)E(G_{1}) is nonempty, guaranteeing surjectivity. An example of such a construction is shown in Fig. 3.1 where n=12n=12, r=3r=3, and si=4s_{i}=4 for all ii.

The following lemma shows that the wild number of KnK_{n} with a clique-fragmentation coloring is determined by the number of parts in the vertex partition of KnK_{n}.

{lemma}

For any clique-fragmentation coloring with rr parts, we have

wld⁡(Kn)=r−1.\wld(K_{n})=r-1.
Proof.

By construction, G1G_{1} consists of rr vertex-disjoint cliques, so κ⁡(G1)=r\kappa(G_{1})=r. Since r≥2r\geq 2 and si≥1s_{i}\geq 1 for all ii, the complete multipartite graph G2G_{2} is connected. Applying (2), we have

wld⁡(Kn)=κ⁡(G1)+κ⁡(G2)−2=r+1−2=r−1.∎\wld(K_{n})=\kappa(G_{1})+\kappa(G_{2})-2=r+1-2=r-1.\qed
3.1.

Let n≥4n\geq 4. For any 22-coloring of KnK_{n},

0≤wld⁡(Kn)≤n−2.0\leq\wld(K_{n})\leq n-2.

Moreover, every integer in this range is attainable by some 22-coloring.

Proof.

The surjectivity of the coloring guarantees that κ⁡(G1)≥1\kappa(G_{1})\geq 1 and κ⁡(G2)≥1\kappa(G_{2})\geq 1. For any graph HH on n≥2n\geq 2 vertices, at least one of HH or its complement H¯\overline{H} is connected. Since G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} are complements of each other, we then have κ⁡(G1)=1\kappa(G_{1})=1 or κ⁡(G2)=1\kappa(G_{2})=1, say κ⁡(G1)=1\kappa(G_{1})=1. A graph on nn vertices containing at least one edge has at most n−1n-1 connected components, so

κ⁡(G1)+κ⁡(G2)≤1+(n−1)=n.\kappa(G_{1})+\kappa(G_{2})\leq 1+(n-1)=n.

From Section 2, it follows that 0≤wld⁡(Kn)≤n−20\leq\wld(K_{n})\leq n-2. Since n≥4n\geq 4, the attainability of the wild number 00 is shown by the coloring discussed at the beginning of this subsection. For 1≤k≤n−21\leq k\leq n-2, choose r=k+1r=k+1 in Section 3.1. Then, by Section 3.1, we have wld⁡(Kn)=r−1=k\wld(K_{n})=r-1=k, verifying the attainability of every wild number in the range {1,…,n−2}\{1,\dots,n-2\}. ∎

3.2 Equitable 22-Colorings

We determine the set of wild numbers attainable by equitable 22-colorings of KnK_{n}. We begin by constructing an equitable 22-coloring that can be defined to achieve any number in the full range of possible wild numbers.

{construction}

Let n≥4n\geq 4 and let m∈{⌊n⁡(n−1)/4⌋,⌈n⁡(n−1)/4⌉}m\in\{\lfloor n(n-1)/4\rfloor,\lceil n(n-1)/4\rceil\}. Set t=⌈1+1+8​m2⌉t=\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{1+8m}}{2}\right\rceil. Fix mm and let 1≤k≤n−t1\leq k\leq n-t. We construct an equitable 22-coloring such that there is a color class containing mm edges that form k+1k+1 components consisting of one component of size n−kn-k and the remaining components consisting of isolated vertices.

Partition V⁡(Kn)V(K_{n}) into two sets U1U_{1} and V1V_{1} such that |U1|=k|U_{1}|=k and |V1|=n−k|V_{1}|=n-k. Choose a spanning tree of Kn​[V1]K_{n}[V_{1}], and then add further edges of Kn​[V1]K_{n}[V_{1}] until the subgraph has mm edges. Existence of mm edges is guaranteed since k≤n−tk\leq n-t gives n−k≥tn-k\geq t, and so (n−k2)≥(t2)≥m\binom{n-k}{2}\geq\binom{t}{2}\geq m. Connectedness is guaranteed, since n≥4n\geq 4, by m≥⌊n⁡(n−1)/4⌋≥n−2≥n−k−1m\geq\lfloor n(n-1)/4\rfloor\geq n-2\geq n-k-1.

Let this set of mm edges be M⊂E⁡(Kn)M\subset E(K_{n}). Define a 22-coloring γ\gamma such that:

  • •

    G1G_{1} is the graph with vertex set V⁡(Kn)V(K_{n}) and edge set MM.

  • •

    G2G_{2} is the graph with vertex set V⁡(Kn)V(K_{n}) and edge set E⁡(Kn)∖ME(K_{n})\setminus M.

Note that κ⁡(G1)=k+1\kappa(G_{1})=k+1 and κ⁡(G2)=1\kappa(G_{2})=1 since G2G_{2} contains every edge between U1U_{1} and V1V_{1}. An example of Section 3.2 is shown in Fig. 3.2 for n=12n=12, m=33m=33, and k=n−t=3k=n-t=3.

{lemma}

Let n≥4n\geq 4 and let m∈{⌊n⁡(n−1)/4⌋,⌈n⁡(n−1)/4⌉}m\in\{\lfloor n(n-1)/4\rfloor,\lceil n(n-1)/4\rceil\}. Fix mm and let 1≤k≤n−⌈1+1+8​m2⌉1\leq k\leq n-\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{1+8m}}{2}\right\rceil. Section 3.2 defines an equitable 22-coloring ε\varepsilon such that

wldε⁡(Kn)=k.\wld_{\varepsilon}(K_{n})=k.
Proof.

By construction, G1G_{1} consists of k+1k+1 components and G2G_{2} is connected. From (2), as ε\varepsilon is a 22-coloring, it follows that wldε⁡(Kn)=κ⁡(G1)+κ⁡(G2)−2=(k+1)+1−2=k\wld_{\varepsilon}(K_{n})=\kappa(G_{1})+\kappa(G_{2})-2=(k+1)+1-2=k. ∎

3.2.

Let n≥4n\geq 4. For any equitable 22-coloring of the edges of KnK_{n}, if both color classes are connected, then

wld⁡(Kn)=0.\wld(K_{n})=0.

Otherwise, let m∈{⌊n⁡(n−1)/4⌋,⌈n⁡(n−1)/4⌉}m\in\{\lfloor n(n-1)/4\rfloor,\lceil n(n-1)/4\rceil\} be the number of edges in a disconnected color class. Then

1≤wld⁡(Kn)≤n−⌈1+1+8​m2⌉.1\leq\wld(K_{n})\leq n-\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{1+8m}}{2}\right\rceil.

Moreover, every integer from 00 to n−⌈1+1+8​m2⌉n-\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{1+8m}}{2}\right\rceil is attainable by some equitable 22-coloring.

Proof.

By Section 2, we have

wld⁡(Kn)≤κ⁡(G1)+κ⁡(G2)−2.\wld(K_{n})\leq\kappa(G_{1})+\kappa(G_{2})-2. (3)

Since G2=G1¯G_{2}=\overline{G_{1}}, at most one of {G1,G2}\{G_{1},G_{2}\} is disconnected. If both are connected, then (3) gives wld⁡(Kn)=0\wld(K_{n})=0. For the remainder of the proof, we may assume without loss of generality that κ⁡(G1)>1\kappa(G_{1})>1 and κ⁡(G2)=1\kappa(G_{2})=1. Set m=|E⁡(G1)|m=|E(G_{1})|; then m∈{⌊n⁡(n−1)/4⌋,⌈n⁡(n−1)/4⌉}m\in\{\lfloor n(n-1)/4\rfloor,\lceil n(n-1)/4\rceil\} and |E⁡(G2)|=(n2)−m|E(G_{2})|=\binom{n}{2}-m. Now we bound the number of components in G1G_{1}.

Let κ⁡(G1)=q\kappa(G_{1})=q with components of size a1,a2,…,aqa_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{q} where ∑i=1qai=n\sum_{i=1}^{q}a_{i}=n and each ai>0a_{i}>0. The maximum number of edges in a component on aia_{i} vertices is (ai2)\binom{a_{i}}{2}, so

m≤∑i=1q(ai2).\displaystyle m\leq\sum_{i=1}^{q}\binom{a_{i}}{2}.

Since x↦(x2)x\mapsto\binom{x}{2} is convex, this sum is maximized when the component sizes are as unequal as possible, namely when one component contains n−q+1n-q+1 vertices and the remaining q−1q-1 components are isolated vertices. Thus,

m≤∑i=1q(ai2)≤(n−q+12).m\leq\sum_{i=1}^{q}\binom{a_{i}}{2}\leq\binom{n-q+1}{2}.

Let t=min⁡{s:(s2)≥m}t=\min\{s:\binom{s}{2}\geq m\}. Then t≤n−q+1t\leq n-q+1 and q≤n−t+1q\leq n-t+1. Since t=min⁡{s:(s2)≥m}t=\min\{s:\binom{s}{2}\geq m\}, we have (t2)=t⁡(t−1)2≥m\binom{t}{2}=\frac{t(t-1)}{2}\geq m and thus t≥1+1+8​m2t\geq\frac{1+\sqrt{1+8m}}{2}. By minimality, it follows that t=⌈1+1+8​m2⌉t=\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{1+8m}}{2}\right\rceil. From (3), we have

wld⁡(Kn)≤q−1≤n−t=n−⌈1+1+8​m2⌉.\wld(K_{n})\leq q-1\leq n-t=n-\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{1+8m}}{2}\right\rceil.

Recall that the spanning tree packing number of KnK_{n} is ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor, so for n≥4n\geq 4 there are at least two edge-disjoint spanning trees in KnK_{n}. Assigning a spanning tree to each color class and partitioning the remaining edges in an equitable way verifies the attainability of wild number 00. For all 1≤k≤n−⌈1+1+8​m2⌉1\leq k\leq n-\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{1+8m}}{2}\right\rceil, Section 3.2 and Section 3.2 ensure that wldε⁡(Kn)=k\wld_{\varepsilon}(K_{n})=k, verifying the attainability of every wild number in the range of {1,…,n−⌈1+1+8​m2⌉}\{1,\dots,n-\left\lceil\frac{1+\sqrt{1+8m}}{2}\right\rceil\}. ∎

Note that for all n≥4n\geq 4, we can simplify the bound to 0≤wld⁡(Kn)≤(1−2/2)​n+3/20\leq\wld(K_{n})\leq(1-\sqrt{2}/2)\,n+3/2.

3.2.1 Expected Wild Number

As shown above, every wild number in the attainable range for an equitable 22-coloring of KnK_{n} occurs. However, the expected wild number for a uniformly random equitable 22-coloring of K4K_{4} is only 2/52/5. We show that, as nn grows, the expected wild number of a uniformly random equitable 22-coloring of KnK_{n} tends to 00. The following lemma is an immediate consequence of Gilbert’s bounds on the connectivity probability.

{lemma}

[[9]] Let GG be the random graph on nn vertices where every edge occurs independently with probability 1/21/2. Then Pr⁡[G​ is disconnected]=O⁡(n​2−n)\Pr[G\text{ is disconnected}]=O(n2^{-n}).

{corollary}

Let N=(n2)N=\binom{n}{2} and let M∈{⌊N/2⌋,⌈N/2⌉}M\in\{\lfloor N/2\rfloor,\lceil N/2\rceil\}. If Gn,MG_{n,M} is chosen uniformly from all graphs on nn vertices with MM edges, then

Pr⁡[Gn,M​ is disconnected]=o⁡(1/n).\Pr[G_{n,M}\text{ is disconnected}]=o(1/n).
Proof.

Let GG be the random graph on nn vertices where every edge occurs independently with probability 1/21/2. Conditional on |E⁡(G)|=M|E(G)|=M, the graph GG is uniformly distributed over all graphs on nn vertices with exactly MM edges. It follows that

Pr⁡[Gn,M​ is disconnected]\displaystyle\Pr[G_{n,M}\text{ is disconnected}] =Pr⁡[G​ is disconnected∣|E⁡(G)|=M]\displaystyle=\Pr[G\text{ is disconnected}\mid|E(G)|=M]
≤Pr⁡[G​ is disconnected]Pr[|E(G)|=M]\displaystyle\leq\frac{\Pr[G\text{ is disconnected}]}{\Pr[|E(G)|=M]}
=Pr⁡[G​ is disconnected]2−N​(NM)\displaystyle=\frac{\Pr[G\text{ is disconnected}]}{2^{-N}\binom{N}{M}}

From Section 3.2.1, we have Pr⁡[G​ is disconnected]=O⁡(n​2−n)\Pr[G\text{ is disconnected}]=O(n2^{-n}). Applying Stirling’s approximation to the central binomial coefficient, we have

2−N(NM)=Θ(N−1/2)=Θ(1/n)2^{-N}\binom{N}{M}=\Theta(N^{-1/2})=\Theta(1/n)

since |M−N/2|=O⁡(N)|M-N/2|=O(\sqrt{N}). Therefore

Pr⁡[Gn,M​ is disconnected]=O⁡(n​2−n)Θ⁡(1/n)=O⁡(n2​2−n)=o⁡(1/n).∎\Pr[G_{n,M}\text{ is disconnected}]=\frac{O(n2^{-n})}{\Theta(1/n)}=O(n^{2}2^{-n})=o(1/n).\qed
3.3.

Let ε\varepsilon be a uniformly random equitable 22-coloring of KnK_{n}. Then 𝔼⁡[wldε⁡(Kn)]→0\mathbb{E}[\wld_{\varepsilon}(K_{n})]\to 0 as n→∞n\to\infty.

Proof.

Let N=(n2)N=\binom{n}{2}. Since ε\varepsilon is equitable, for i=1,2i=1,2, we have |E⁡(Gi)|∈{⌊N/2⌋,⌈N/2⌉}|E(G_{i})|\in\{\lfloor N/2\rfloor,\lceil N/2\rceil\}. From (2), the wild number of KnK_{n} with ε\varepsilon is

wld⁡(Kn)=(κ⁡(G1)−1)+(κ⁡(G2)−1).\wld(K_{n})=(\kappa(G_{1})-1)+(\kappa(G_{2})-1).

The expected wild number of KnK_{n} is then

𝔼⁡[wld⁡(Kn)]=𝔼⁡[κ⁡(G1)−1]+𝔼⁡[κ⁡(G2)−1].\mathbb{E}[\wld(K_{n})]=\mathbb{E}[\kappa(G_{1})-1]+\mathbb{E}[\kappa(G_{2})-1].

Conditional on its number of edges, each GiG_{i} is uniformly distributed over all graphs on nn vertices with that many edges. Since a graph on nn vertices can have at most nn components, for i=1,2i=1,2, we then have

𝔼⁡[κ⁡(Gi)−1]≤(n−1)​Pr⁡[Gi​ is disconnected]=o⁡(1)\mathbb{E}[\kappa(G_{i})-1]\leq(n-1)\Pr[G_{i}\text{ is disconnected}]=o(1)

by Section 3.2.1. Thus,

𝔼⁡[wld⁡(Kn)]=𝔼⁡[κ⁡(G1)−1]+𝔼⁡[κ⁡(G2)−1]=o⁡(1)⟶0.∎\mathbb{E}[\wld(K_{n})]=\mathbb{E}[\kappa(G_{1})-1]+\mathbb{E}[\kappa(G_{2})-1]=o(1)\longrightarrow 0.\qed

3.3 Minimum Proper Colorings

When nn is odd, χ′​(Kn)=n\chi^{\prime}(K_{n})=n and every color class is a near-perfect matching of size (n−1)/2(n-1)/2; when nn is even, χ′​(Kn)=n−1\chi^{\prime}(K_{n})=n-1 and every color class is a perfect matching of size n/2n/2. For a color cic_{i}, we write MiM_{i} for its monochromatic matching. For odd nn, we denote the isolated vertex in color cic_{i} by viv_{i}. Note that each color misses exactly one vertex, and each vertex misses exactly one color, so ci↦vic_{i}\mapsto v_{i} is a bijection between colors and vertices; in particular, the viv_{i} are distinct.

For minimum proper colorings of KnK_{n}, ideal wild sets satisfy several structural constraints that will be used throughout this section.

{lemma}

Let n≥3n\geq 3 and let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n}. Every color-connecting set is incident to at least n−1n-1 vertices, and to all nn vertices when nn is odd. Moreover, every ideal wild set is a forest in which every nontrivial component has at least three vertices.

Proof.

First, any color-connecting set must be incident to at least n−1n-1 vertices. Indeed, if two vertices are not incident to any wild edge, then the unique edge joining them is isolated in its color class, preventing that color class from becoming connected. When nn is odd, each color class is a near-perfect matching with a unique isolated vertex. Consequently, every vertex must be incident to a wild edge, as an isolated vertex would remain isolated in its missing color.

Minimality of an ideal wild set further implies that every ideal wild set is a forest. If an edge ee lies on a cycle of a color-connecting set WW, then the endpoints of ee remain joined by a path in W−eW-e, thus GiW−eG_{i}^{W-e} would remain connected for all ii implying W−eW-e is a color-connecting set. By the same argument as above, no component formed by the edges of an ideal wild set can be a single edge as the edge would remain isolated in its own color class. Thus, every nontrivial component contains at least three vertices. ∎

3.3.1 Lower Bound

The properties of ideal wild sets discussed above provide a natural lower bound on the wild number.

3.4.

For any minimum proper coloring ρ\rho of KnK_{n} with n≥3n\geq 3, the wild number satisfies

wldρ⁡(Kn)≥⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋.\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\geq\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\rfloor.
Proof.

Let WW be an ideal wild set. Let ss be the number of vertices incident to an edge in WW. By Section 3.3, we have s≥n−1s\geq n-1 if nn is even and s=ns=n if nn is odd. In all cases, s≥2​⌈n/2⌉−1s\geq 2\lceil n/2\rceil-1. Further, we have that WW is a forest on ss vertices. Let tt be the number of tree components of WW. Since each component contains at least 33 vertices, by Section 3.3, we have t≤⌊s/3⌋t\leq\lfloor s/3\rfloor so |W|=s−t≥s−⌊s/3⌋|W|=s-t\geq s-\lfloor s/3\rfloor. Note that the function f⁡(x)=x−⌊x/3⌋f(x)=x-\lfloor x/3\rfloor is non-decreasing on the integers. Since s≥2​⌈n/2⌉−1s\geq 2\lceil n/2\rceil-1, we have

|W|≥(2​⌈n/2⌉−1)−⌊2​⌈n/2⌉−13⌋.|W|\geq\bigl(2\lceil n/2\rceil-1\bigr)-\left\lfloor\frac{2\lceil n/2\rceil-1}{3}\right\rfloor.

Setting k=⌈n/2⌉k=\lceil n/2\rceil and writing k=3​q+rk=3q+r with r∈{0,1,2}r\in\{0,1,2\}, both 2​k−1−⌊(2​k−1)/3⌋2k-1-\lfloor(2k-1)/3\rfloor and ⌊4​k/3⌋\lfloor 4k/3\rfloor equal 4​q+r4q+r. Therefore, |W|≥⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋|W|\geq\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor and so

wldρ⁡(Kn)≥⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋.∎\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\geq\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor.\qed

3.3.2 Structure of Ideal Wild Sets

Recall that viv_{i} is the vertex isolated in color cic_{i}. We call a set T={vi,vj,vk}⊆V⁡(Kn)T=\{v_{i},v_{j},v_{k}\}\subseteq V(K_{n}) a valid triple if ρ⁡(vj​vk)≠ci\rho(v_{j}v_{k})\neq c_{i}, ρ⁡(vi​vk)≠cj\rho(v_{i}v_{k})\neq c_{j}, and ρ⁡(vi​vj)≠ck\rho(v_{i}v_{j})\neq c_{k}. This condition is necessary for TT to occur as a component of a color-connecting set, since otherwise there would be no edge of color cic_{i}, cjc_{j}, or ckc_{k} connecting TT to the remaining vertices. We call TT invalid for cic_{i} if TT is not a valid triple because ρ⁡(vj​vk)=ci\rho(v_{j}v_{k})=c_{i}, or simply invalid when color does not matter.

{lemma}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n}. For odd n≥7n\geq 7, the graph KnK_{n} contains a valid triple.

Proof.

Each edge x​y∈Mixy\in M_{i} witnesses the invalid triple {vi,x,y}\{v_{i},x,y\}. Conversely, every invalid triple is witnessed by at least one of the edges between its vertices.

An edge witnesses exactly one invalid triple, since its color cic_{i} determines a unique vertex viv_{i}. Therefore, the number of invalid triples is at most |E⁡(Kn)|=(n2)|E(K_{n})|=\binom{n}{2}. Since n≥7n\geq 7, the number of total triples, (n3)\binom{n}{3}, exceeds (n2)\binom{n}{2}. Hence not every triple is invalid, and a valid triple exists. ∎

When nn is odd, Section 3.3 implies that any ideal wild set must be a spanning forest where every component contains at least 33 vertices. We call the vertex sets of these components blocks.

A forest of blocks fails to be color-connecting when a nonempty union of blocks is closed under some color class and is, therefore, disconnected from the remaining blocks. We isolate this obstruction in the following definition.

{definition}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n} with nn odd, and let P={B1,…,Bt}P=\{B_{1},\dots,B_{t}\} be a partition of V⁡(Kn)V(K_{n}) into blocks where |Bj|≥3|B_{j}|\geq 3 for 1≤j≤t1\leq j\leq t. A seal is a pair (ci,𝒰)(c_{i},\mathcal{U}), where cic_{i} is a color and 𝒰⊆P\mathcal{U}\subseteq P is a nonempty set of blocks whose vertex union U=⋃B∈𝒰BU=\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal{U}}B satisfies:

  1. (i)

    vi∉Uv_{i}\notin U, and

  2. (ii)

    every edge of MiM_{i} with an endpoint in UU has both endpoints in UU; equivalently, MiM_{i} restricted to UU is a perfect matching of UU.

We call PP seal-free if it admits no seal. Since a perfect matching requires an even number of vertices, |U||U| is even for every seal; in particular, a single odd block cannot by itself form a seal. Up to relabeling, the two possible seals consisting of two triples are shown in Fig. 3.3.

{proposition}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n} with nn odd and let P={B1,…,Bt}P=\{B_{1},\dots,B_{t}\} be a partition of V⁡(Kn)V(K_{n}) into blocks where |Bj|≥3|B_{j}|\geq 3 for 1≤j≤t1\leq j\leq t. For each jj, let TjT_{j} be a spanning tree of Kn​[Bj]K_{n}[B_{j}], and let W=∪j=1tE(Tj)W=\cup_{j=1}^{t}E(T_{j}). Then WW is color-connecting if and only if PP is seal-free.

Proof.

First, suppose PP has a seal (ci,𝒰)(c_{i},\mathcal{U}), with U=⋃B∈𝒰BU=\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal{U}}B and U¯=V⁡(Kn)−U\overline{U}=V(K_{n})-U. We claim no edge of GiWG_{i}^{W}, whose edge set is Mi∪WM_{i}\cup W, joins UU to its complement U¯\overline{U}. The blocks of a partition are pairwise disjoint, so every block lies entirely in UU or entirely in U¯\overline{U}. A wild edge e∈We\in W has both endpoints in a single block, and that block lies on one side, so no wild edge crosses the cut (U,U¯)(U,\overline{U}); by condition (ii) of Section 3.3.2, no edge of MiM_{i} crosses either. Both sides are nonempty; U≠∅U\neq\emptyset since 𝒰≠∅\mathcal{U}\neq\emptyset and vi∈U¯v_{i}\in\overline{U} since vi∉Uv_{i}\notin U. So GiWG_{i}^{W} is disconnected and WW is not color-connecting.

Conversely, suppose WW is not color-connecting, say GiWG_{i}^{W} is disconnected for the color cic_{i}. Each block of PP is connected by its wild spanning tree, so every component of GiWG_{i}^{W} is a union of whole blocks. Hence the blocks of PP split into two nonempty sets 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} with no edge of MiM_{i} between A=⋃𝒜A=\bigcup\mathcal{A} and B=⋃ℬB=\bigcup\mathcal{B}. Note that MiM_{i} is a near-perfect matching missing exactly the vertex viv_{i}, which lies in either AA or BB, say vi∈Av_{i}\in A. Then every vertex of BB is matched by MiM_{i}, and since no edge colored cic_{i} has exactly one endpoint in BB, it has both endpoints in BB. Thus MiM_{i} restricted to BB is a perfect matching, and (ci,ℬ)(c_{i},\mathcal{B}) is a seal. Note that neither direction referred to the choice of spanning trees inside the blocks, so color-connectivity depends only on the partition. ∎

{lemma}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n} with n≥7n\geq 7 odd, and let A⊆V⁡(Kn)A\subseteq V(K_{n}) where |A|=4|A|=4. If AA is a block of a partition PP, then (ci,{A})(c_{i},\{A\}) is not a seal for any ii if and only if Kn​[A]K_{n}[A] is a rainbow K4K_{4}.

Proof.

Since ρ\rho is proper, if some color cic_{i} appears twice in Kn​[A]K_{n}[A], the two edges colored cic_{i} are disjoint and cover AA; hence vi∉Av_{i}\notin A and (ci,{A})(c_{i},\{A\}) is a seal. Conversely, since |A|=4|A|=4, a seal (ci,{A})(c_{i},\{A\}) is a pair of disjoint edges colored cic_{i} between the vertices of AA, so cic_{i} is a repeated color. Thus, a seal (ci,{A})(c_{i},\{A\}) exists for some cic_{i} if and only if Kn​[A]K_{n}[A] is not rainbow. ∎

{lemma}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n} with n≥7n\geq 7 odd, and let PP be a partition of V⁡(Kn)V(K_{n}) into blocks, one of which is a triple TT. Let 𝒰=P∖{T}\mathcal{U}=P\setminus\{T\}. Then (ci,𝒰)(c_{i},\mathcal{U}) is a seal if and only if TT is invalid for cic_{i}.

Proof.

Suppose (ci,𝒰)(c_{i},\mathcal{U}) is a seal. By definition, vi∉Uv_{i}\notin U, so vi∈Tv_{i}\in T. Since |T|=3|T|=3, the remaining set U=V⁡(Kn)∖TU=V(K_{n})\setminus T contains n−3n-3 vertices. Since MiM_{i} restricted to UU is a perfect matching of UU, it uses (n−3)/2(n-3)/2 edges of MiM_{i}, so exactly (n−1)/2−(n−3)/2=1(n-1)/2-(n-3)/2=1 edge of MiM_{i} remains. Since every vertex of UU is already matched, this edge has no endpoint in UU. Thus it must have both endpoints in T∖{vi}T\setminus\{v_{i}\}. It follows that TT contains the isolated vertex viv_{i} and its other two vertices are joined by an edge colored cic_{i}, making TT invalid for cic_{i}.

Conversely, if TT is invalid for cic_{i}, then T={vi,a,b}T=\{v_{i},a,b\} with ρ⁡(a​b)=ci\rho(ab)=c_{i}. The remaining (n−1)/2−1=(n−3)/2(n-1)/2-1=(n-3)/2 edges of MiM_{i} cover the remaining n−3n-3 vertices of the graph, which are V⁡(Kn)∖T=UV(K_{n})\setminus T=U. Those edges form a perfect matching of UU. Thus, (ci,𝒰)(c_{i},\mathcal{U}) is a seal. ∎

3.3.3 Small Cases

The following lemma allows us to bound the wild number of an even complete graph by an odd complete graph.

{lemma}

Let k≥2k\geq 2, let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of K2​kK_{2k}, and let v∈V⁡(K2​k)v\in V(K_{2k}). Define

ρv:=ρ|K2​k−v.\rho_{v}:=\rho|_{K_{2k}-v}.

Then ρv\rho_{v} is a minimum proper coloring of K2​k−1K_{2k-1} and

wldρ⁡(K2​k)≤wldρv⁡(K2​k−1).\wld_{\rho}(K_{2k})\leq\wld_{\rho_{v}}(K_{2k-1}).
Proof.

The coloring ρ\rho uses 2​k−12k-1 colors, and each color class is a perfect matching of size kk. Deleting vv removes exactly one edge from each color class. Thus every color class of ρv\rho_{v} is a near-perfect matching of size k−1k-1 and ρv\rho_{v} is a proper coloring of K2​k−1K_{2k-1} using 2​k−12k-1 colors, and so is minimum as χ′​(K2​k−1)=2​k−1\chi^{\prime}(K_{2k-1})=2k-1.

Let W⊆E⁡(K2​k−v)W\subseteq E(K_{2k}-v) be color-connecting under ρv\rho_{v}. Fix a color cic_{i} and let eie_{i} be the unique edge of MiM_{i} incident to vv. The graph (Mi−ei)∪W(M_{i}-e_{i})\cup W is connected on V⁡(K2​k−v)V(K_{2k}-v) and eie_{i} joins vv to a vertex of (Mi−ei)∪W(M_{i}-e_{i})\cup W. Hence Mi∪WM_{i}\cup W is connected on V⁡(K2​k)V(K_{2k}).

This holds for every color cic_{i}, so WW is also color-connecting in K2​kK_{2k}. Therefore,

wldρ⁡(K2​k)≤wldρv⁡(K2​k−1).∎\wld_{\rho}(K_{2k})\leq\wld_{\rho_{v}}(K_{2k-1}).\qed
{lemma}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of K7K_{7}. Suppose that TT is a valid triple and that BB induces a rainbow K4K_{4} and is disjoint from TT. Then the union of the spanning trees of K7​[T]K_{7}[T] and K7​[B]K_{7}[B] is a color-connecting set of size 55.

Proof.

Note that P={T,B}P=\{T,B\} is a block partition of V⁡(K7)V(K_{7}) and WW, consisting of a spanning tree of each block, has |W|=(3−1)+(4−1)=5|W|=(3-1)+(4-1)=5. By Section 3.3.2, WW is color-connecting if the partition PP admits no seals. Recall that a seal perfectly matches its vertices, requiring an even number of vertices. The only nonempty subset of PP whose union has even size is {B}\{B\}. By Section 3.3.2, (ci,{B})(c_{i},\{B\}) is a seal for some cic_{i} if and only if K7​[B]K_{7}[B] is not rainbow. From our assumptions, we have that K7​[B]K_{7}[B] is rainbow, so no seal has the form (ci,{B})(c_{i},\{B\}). Thus, WW is color-connecting. ∎

{lemma}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of K9K_{9}. Then we can partition V⁡(K9)V(K_{9}) into three valid triples.

Proof.

By Section 3.3.2, there is a valid triple; relabel so that it is T={v1,v2,v3}T=\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\}. Each edge vj​vkv_{j}v_{k} of TT is not colored cjc_{j} or ckc_{k}, since vjv_{j} and vkv_{k} are isolated in those colors, and is not colored cic_{i}, since TT is valid. As ρ\rho is proper, the three edges of TT receive distinct colors, which we relabel c4,c5,c6c_{4},c_{5},c_{6}. It remains to partition the remaining six vertices into two valid triples. There are (63)/2=10\binom{6}{3}/2=10 ways to partition the remaining six vertices into two unordered triples.

We now bound the number of partitions that do not produce the remaining two valid triples. Since v1,v2,v3∈Tv_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\in T, no invalid triple among the remaining six vertices can arise from colors c1,c2,c3c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}. For {c4,c5,c6}\{c_{4},c_{5},c_{6}\}, one matching edge lies inside TT, and the third vertex of TT is matched outside TT, leaving two matching edges among the remaining six vertices. Thus, at most 22 remaining edges of each color can contribute invalid triples. For {c7,c8,c9}\{c_{7},c_{8},c_{9}\}, no matching edge lies inside TT, so the three vertices of TT are matched to three vertices outside TT, leaving one matching edge among the remaining six vertices. Thus, at most 11 remaining edge of each color can contribute invalid triples. Therefore, among the remaining six vertices, there are at most 3⋅2+3⋅1=93\cdot 2+3\cdot 1=9 invalid triples.

Each invalid triple determines at most one partition of the remaining six vertices that does not produce the two remaining valid triples, namely the partition consisting of that triple and its complement. Therefore, at most 99 of the 1010 partitions are invalid. Hence at least one partition of the remaining six vertices consists of two valid triples. TT together with these two valid triples gives a partition of V⁡(K9)V(K_{9}) into three valid triples. ∎

{lemma}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of K9K_{9}. Suppose that T1,T2,T3⊆V⁡(K9)T_{1},T_{2},T_{3}\subseteq V(K_{9}) are valid triples such that T1,T2,T3T_{1},T_{2},T_{3} are pairwise disjoint. Then the union of the spanning trees of K9​[T1],K9​[T2]K_{9}[T_{1}],K_{9}[T_{2}], and K9​[T3]K_{9}[T_{3}] is a color-connecting set of size 66.

Proof.

Note that P={T1,T2,T3}P=\{T_{1},T_{2},T_{3}\} is a block partition of V⁡(K9)V(K_{9}), and by Section 3.3.2, it suffices to rule out the existence of seals. The union of blocks in a seal contains an even number of vertices, so 𝒰\mathcal{U} must consist of exactly two triples. By Section 3.3.2, a seal (ci,P∖{Tj})(c_{i},P\setminus\{T_{j}\}) exists exactly when TjT_{j} is invalid for cic_{i}. Let WW be the union of the spanning trees of K9​[T1],K9​[T2]K_{9}[T_{1}],K_{9}[T_{2}], and K9​[T3]K_{9}[T_{3}]. All three triples are valid, so PP is seal-free and WW is color-connecting with |W|=3​(3−1)=6|W|=3(3-1)=6. ∎

{lemma}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of K11K_{11}. Then we can partition V⁡(K11)V(K_{11}) into a valid triple TT and two blocks that each induce a rainbow K4K_{4}.

Proof.

By Section 3.3.2, there is a valid triple; relabel so that it is T={v1,v2,v3}T=\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\}. Each edge vj​vkv_{j}v_{k} of TT is not colored cjc_{j} or ckc_{k}, since vjv_{j} and vkv_{k} are isolated in those colors, and is not colored cic_{i}, since TT is valid. As ρ\rho is proper, the three edges of TT receive distinct colors, which we relabel c4,c5,c6c_{4},c_{5},c_{6}. It remains to partition the remaining eight vertices into two sets, each inducing a rainbow K4K_{4}. There are (84)/2=35\binom{8}{4}/2=35 partitions of these eight vertices into two sets of size 44.

For the colors {c1,c2,c3}\{c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}\}, one vertex of TT is missed, while the other two vertices of TT are matched to vertices outside TT, since TT is valid. Thus, two edges of each such color are incident to TT, leaving 5−2=35-2=3 edges among the remaining eight vertices. For {c4,c5,c6}\{c_{4},c_{5},c_{6}\}, one edge of each color lies inside TT, while the remaining vertex of TT is matched to a vertex outside TT. Thus, again, two edges of each such color are incident to TT, leaving 5−2=35-2=3 edges among the remaining eight vertices. For {c7,…,c11}\{c_{7},\dots,c_{11}\}, no edge lies inside TT and no vertex of TT is missed, so all three vertices of TT are matched to vertices outside TT. Thus, there are 5−3=25-3=2 edges of each such color among the remaining eight vertices.

We now bound the number of partitions that do not produce two disjoint rainbow K4K_{4}. For {c1,…,c6}\{c_{1},\dots,c_{6}\}, there are 33 matching edges among the remaining eight vertices. A 44-set on which color cic_{i} appears twice is the vertex set of a pair of these edges, so each such color yields at most (32)=3\binom{3}{2}=3 non-rainbow 44-sets, for at most 6⋅3=186\cdot 3=18 in total. For {c7,…,c11}\{c_{7},\dots,c_{11}\}, there are exactly two matching edges among the remaining eight vertices, and these determine a unique non-rainbow K4K_{4}. Thus, these five colors produce at most 55 additional K4K_{4} that are not rainbow. Each K4K_{4} that is not rainbow determines a unique unordered partition of the remaining eight vertices into two sets of size 44. Since the total number of bad partitions is at most 18+5=23<3518+5=23<35, we have at least one partition into two disjoint rainbow K4K_{4}. ∎

{lemma}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of K11K_{11}. Suppose that T⊆V⁡(K11)T\subseteq V(K_{11}) is a valid triple and that B1,B2⊆V⁡(K11)B_{1},B_{2}\subseteq V(K_{11}) each induce a rainbow K4K_{4} such that T,B1,B2T,B_{1},B_{2} are pairwise disjoint. Then the union of the spanning trees of K11​[T],K11​[B1]K_{11}[T],K_{11}[B_{1}], and K11​[B2]K_{11}[B_{2}] is a color-connecting set of size 88.

Proof.

Note that P={T,B1,B2}P=\{T,B_{1},B_{2}\} is a block partition of V⁡(K11)V(K_{11}), and by Section 3.3.2, it suffices to rule out the existence of seals. Recall that a seal requires an even number of vertices, so we need only consider the sets {B1}\{B_{1}\}, {B2}\{B_{2}\}, and {B1,B2}\{B_{1},B_{2}\}. By Section 3.3.2, a seal on {B1}\{B_{1}\} or {B2}\{B_{2}\} exists exactly when the corresponding K4K_{4} is not rainbow. By Section 3.3.2, a seal on {B1,B2}=P∖{T}\{B_{1},B_{2}\}=P\setminus\{T\} exists exactly when TT is invalid. So PP is seal-free when TT is valid and K11​[B1],K11​[B2]K_{11}[B_{1}],K_{11}[B_{2}] are rainbow. Let WW be the union of the spanning trees of K11​[T],K11​[B1]K_{11}[T],K_{11}[B_{1}], and K11​[B2]K_{11}[B_{2}], so |W|=(3−1)+(4−1)+(4−1)=8|W|=(3-1)+(4-1)+(4-1)=8. By Section 3.3.2, it follows that WW is color-connecting when TT is valid and K11​[B1],K11​[B2]K_{11}[B_{1}],K_{11}[B_{2}] are rainbow. ∎

3.5.

Let 3≤n≤123\leq n\leq 12 and let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n}. Then

wldρ⁡(Kn)=⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋.\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})=\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor.
Proof.

Given a minimum proper coloring ρ\rho of KnK_{n}, Theorem 3.4 establishes that

wldρ⁡(Kn)≥⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋.\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\geq\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor.

We show that this lower bound is sharp for 3≤n≤123\leq n\leq 12. We first consider odd nn with 3≤n≤113\leq n\leq 11.

For n∈{3,5}n\in\{3,5\}, the general bound wldρ⁡(Kn)≤n−1\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\leq n-1 from Eq. 1 gives

wldρ⁡(K3)≤2​ and ​wldρ⁡(K5)≤4,\wld_{\rho}(K_{3})\leq 2\text{ and }\wld_{\rho}(K_{5})\leq 4,

which equal the respective lower bounds.

For n=7n=7, by Section 3.3.2, there exists a valid triple T⊆V⁡(K7)T\subseteq V(K_{7}). Let B=V⁡(K7)∖TB=V(K_{7})\setminus T, so |B|=4|B|=4. By Section 3.3.2, a seal of the form (ci,{B})(c_{i},\{B\}) exists if and only if TT is invalid. Since TT is valid, the partition P={T,B}P=\{T,B\} is seal-free. Equivalently, by Section 3.3.2, K7​[B]K_{7}[B] is rainbow. Choosing a spanning tree in each block forms a color-connecting set of size (3−1)+(4−1)=5(3-1)+(4-1)=5 by Section 3.3.3, so

wldρ⁡(K7)≤5.\wld_{\rho}(K_{7})\leq 5.

For n=9n=9, by Section 3.3.3, there exists a partition of V⁡(K9)V(K_{9}) into three disjoint valid triples T1,T2,T3T_{1},T_{2},T_{3}. By Section 3.3.3, the union of the spanning trees of K9​[T1],K9​[T2]K_{9}[T_{1}],K_{9}[T_{2}], and K9​[T3]K_{9}[T_{3}] forms a color-connecting set WW of size |W|=3⋅2=6|W|=3\cdot 2=6. Thus,

wldρ⁡(K9)≤6.\wld_{\rho}(K_{9})\leq 6.

For n=11n=11, by Section 3.3.3, we have a partition of V⁡(K11)V(K_{11}) into T,B1,B2T,B_{1},B_{2} where TT is a valid triple and B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} induce rainbow K4K_{4}. By Section 3.3.3, T,B1,B2T,B_{1},B_{2} form the components of a color-connecting set WW for K11K_{11} with |W|=8|W|=8. Thus,

wldρ⁡(K11)≤8.\wld_{\rho}(K_{11})\leq 8.

These inequalities agree with the respective lower bounds, completing the proof for odd nn with 3≤n≤113\leq n\leq 11.

We now consider even nn with 4≤n≤124\leq n\leq 12 . Choose v∈V⁡(Kn)v\in V(K_{n}), then, by Section 3.3.3, the restriction ρv\rho_{v} is a minimum proper coloring of Kn−1K_{n-1} and

wldρ⁡(Kn)≤wldρv⁡(Kn−1)=⌊4​⌈(n−1)/2⌉3⌋=⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋,\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\leq\wld_{\rho_{v}}(K_{n-1})=\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor,

where the last equality holds since nn is even. By the odd cases established above, the lower bound completes the proof for even nn with 4≤n≤124\leq n\leq 12. ∎

3.3.4 Weak Upper Bound

{lemma}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n} with nn odd and let T⊆V⁡(Kn)T\subseteq V(K_{n}) with |T|=3|T|=3.

  1. (i)

    If vi∉Tv_{i}\notin T, then KnK_{n} has an edge of color cic_{i} with exactly one endpoint in TT.

  2. (ii)

    If T={vi,a,b}T=\{v_{i},a,b\}, then KnK_{n} has an edge of color cic_{i} with exactly one endpoint in TT if and only if ρ⁡(a​b)≠ci\rho(ab)\neq c_{i}.

Proof.

Since nn is odd, MiM_{i} is a near-perfect matching covering every vertex except viv_{i}. We seek an edge colored cic_{i} with exactly one endpoint in TT.

To prove (i), suppose vi∉Tv_{i}\notin T, so all three vertices of TT are matched by MiM_{i}. Since a set of three vertices can contain at most one edge of the matching MiM_{i}, at least one vertex of TT is matched by MiM_{i} to a vertex outside TT.

To prove (ii), suppose T={vi,a,b}T=\{v_{i},a,b\}. The vertex viv_{i} is isolated in MiM_{i}, while each of aa and bb is incident to exactly one edge of MiM_{i}. These edges have both of their endpoints in TT if and only if aa and bb are adjacent to each other, that is, a​b∈Miab\in M_{i}, or ρ⁡(a​b)=ci\rho(ab)=c_{i}. If ρ⁡(a​b)≠ci\rho(ab)\neq c_{i}, at least one of a,ba,b shares an edge colored cic_{i} with a vertex outside of TT. If instead ρ⁡(a​b)=ci\rho(ab)=c_{i}, then a​bab is the only edge colored cic_{i} incident to TT, so there is no edge colored cic_{i} with exactly one endpoint in TT. ∎

3.6.

Let n≥7n\geq 7 be odd and let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n}. Then

wldρ⁡(Kn)≤n−2.\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\leq n-2.
Proof.

By Section 3.3.2, there exists a valid triple T⊆V⁡(Kn)T\subseteq V(K_{n}). Let B=V⁡(Kn)∖TB=V(K_{n})\setminus T. Choose a spanning tree of Kn​[T]K_{n}[T] and a spanning tree of Kn​[B]K_{n}[B], and let WW be the union of their edges. Then

|W|=(|T|−1)+(|B|−1)=2+(n−4)=n−2.|W|=(|T|-1)+(|B|-1)=2+(n-4)=n-2.

Fix a color cic_{i}. If vi∉Tv_{i}\notin T, then Section 3.3.4(i) gives an edge of color cic_{i} between the vertices of TT and BB. If vi∈Tv_{i}\in T, then the fact that TT is a valid triple together with Section 3.3.4(ii) gives an edge of color cic_{i} between the vertices of TT and BB.

The wild edges make TT and BB each connected, while the edge of color cic_{i} guaranteed by Section 3.3.4 joins the two wild components. Therefore, GiWG_{i}^{W} is connected. Since cic_{i} was arbitrary, WW is color-connecting and we have

wldρ⁡(Kn)≤n−2.∎\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\leq n-2.\qed
{corollary}

Let n≥8n\geq 8 be even, and let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n}. Then

wldρ⁡(Kn)≤n−3.\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\leq n-3.
Proof.

Let v∈V⁡(Kn)v\in V(K_{n}). Combining Section 3.3.3 with Theorem 3.6, since n−1≥7n-1\geq 7 is odd, we have

wldρ⁡(Kn)≤wldρv⁡(Kn−1)≤(n−1)−2=n−3.∎\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\leq\wld_{\rho_{v}}(K_{n-1})\leq(n-1)-2=n-3.\qed

3.3.5 Performance of the Greedy Algorithm

We conclude our study of minimum proper colorings of KnK_{n} considering Algorithm 5.10 of [2], an algorithm that produces a color-connecting set. Given a set WW of edges already colored wild, the dip number of an edge ee is

δW​(e)=∑i=1ℓ(κ⁡(GiW)−κ⁡(GiW∪{e})),\delta_{W}(e)=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\bigl(\kappa(G_{i}^{W})-\kappa(G_{i}^{W\cup\{e\}})\bigr),

the number of colors cic_{i} for which coloring ee wild merges two components of GiWG_{i}^{W}. The greedy algorithm repeatedly selects an edge of maximum dip number until the selected set is color-connecting, breaking ties with the potential rule of [2]; our arguments do not depend on how ties are broken.

While the output of Algorithm 5.10 is not necessarily ideal, the color-connecting set produced is always a forest.

{lemma}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n}, and let WgreedyW_{\mathrm{greedy}} be the output of Algorithm 5.10 of [2]. Then WgreedyW_{\mathrm{greedy}} is acyclic. Consequently, |Wgreedy|≤n−1|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|\leq n-1.

Proof.

Suppose the current selected set of edges is WW and the algorithm has not yet terminated. Then there is a color cic_{i} for which GiWG_{i}^{W} is disconnected. Since KnK_{n} is complete, there is an edge u​vuv joining two distinct components of GiWG_{i}^{W}.

The edge u​vuv cannot have color cic_{i}, otherwise it would already belong to MiM_{i}, contradicting the assumption that its endpoints lie in distinct components of GiWG_{i}^{W}. Thus, coloring u​vuv wild merges two components of GiWG_{i}^{W}, so u​vuv has a positive dip number.

Therefore, whenever the algorithm has not terminated, an edge of positive dip number exists. Since the algorithm selects an edge of maximum dip number, it never selects an edge of dip number zero.

We claim that an edge of positive dip number joins two distinct components of the current selected wild set WW. Suppose instead that the endpoints uu and vv of an edge were already connected by a path in WW. Since W⊆E⁡(GiW)W\subseteq E(G_{i}^{W}) for every color cic_{i}, the vertices uu and vv would already be in the same component of GiWG_{i}^{W} for every color. Adding u​vuv would therefore not merge monochromatic components, so its dip number would be zero.

Thus, every edge selected by the algorithm joins two distinct components of the current selected set. Adding such an edge cannot create a cycle. Since the algorithm begins with an empty set, WgreedyW_{\mathrm{greedy}} is acyclic.

As a forest on at most nn vertices, it has at most n−1n-1 edges. Therefore, |Wgreedy|≤n−1|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|\leq n-1. ∎

{lemma}

Let WW be a color-connecting set for KnK_{n}. If Mi⊆WM_{i}\subseteq W for some color cic_{i}, then the edges of WW form a connected spanning subgraph of KnK_{n}. Consequently, |W|≥n−1|W|\geq n-1.

Proof.

Since WW is color-connecting, the spanning subgraph GiWG_{i}^{W} is connected. By hypothesis, Mi⊆WM_{i}\subseteq W, so E⁡(GiW)=Mi∪W=WE(G_{i}^{W})=M_{i}\cup W=W. Every connected graph on nn vertices has at least n−1n-1 edges, so |W|≥n−1|W|\geq n-1. ∎

3.7.

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n} and let WgreedyW_{\mathrm{greedy}} be the output of Algorithm 5.10 of [2]. For n≥3n\geq 3, we have

|Wgreedy|wldρ⁡(Kn)≤n−1⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋,\frac{|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|}{\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})}\leq\frac{n-1}{\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor},

and

0≤|Wgreedy|−wldρ⁡(Kn)≤n−1−⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋.0\leq|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|-\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\leq n-1-\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor.

In particular, this upper bound on the approximation ratio tends to 3/23/2 as nn tends to infinity.

Proof.

By Section 3.3.5, |Wgreedy|≤n−1|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|\leq n-1. By Theorem 3.4, wldρ⁡(Kn)≥⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋.\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\geq\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor. Combining these inequalities gives

|Wgreedy|wldρ⁡(Kn)≤n−1⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋.\frac{|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|}{\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})}\leq\frac{n-1}{\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor}.

Since WgreedyW_{\mathrm{greedy}} is color-connecting and wldρ⁡(Kn)\wld_{\rho}(K_{n}) is the minimum size of a color-connecting set, we have |Wgreedy|−wldρ⁡(Kn)≥0|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|-\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\geq 0. The preceding upper and lower bounds also give

|Wgreedy|−wldρ⁡(Kn)≤n−1−⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋.|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|-\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\leq n-1-\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor.

Finally, since ⌊4​⌈n/2⌉/3⌋=2​n/3+O⁡(1)\lfloor 4\lceil n/2\rceil/3\rfloor=2n/3+O(1), as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty, we have

n−1⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋⟶32.∎\frac{n-1}{\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor}\longrightarrow\frac{3}{2}.\qed

The following corollary identifies color-class saturation as a structural failure of the greedy algorithm. When saturation occurs, the algorithm returns a spanning tree, which is the largest possible acyclic output, even though a smaller color-connecting set exists whenever n≥7n\geq 7.

{corollary}

Let ρ\rho be a minimum proper coloring of KnK_{n}, and suppose that Algorithm 5.10 of [2] saturates a color class, that is, Mi⊆WgreedyM_{i}\subseteq W_{\mathrm{greedy}} for some color cic_{i}. Then

|Wgreedy|=n−1.|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|=n-1.

In that case, WgreedyW_{\mathrm{greedy}} is not ideal whenever n≥7n\geq 7. More precisely,

|Wgreedy|−wldρ⁡(Kn)≥{1,n≥7​ odd,2,n≥8​ even.|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|-\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\geq\begin{cases}1,&n\geq 7\text{ odd},\\ 2,&n\geq 8\text{ even}.\end{cases}
Proof.

By Section 3.3.5, |Wgreedy|≥n−1|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|\geq n-1. By Section 3.3.5, |Wgreedy|≤n−1|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|\leq n-1. Therefore, |Wgreedy|=n−1|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|=n-1.

Suppose that n≥7n\geq 7 is odd. By Theorem 3.6, wldρ⁡(Kn)≤n−2\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\leq n-2. Thus,

|Wgreedy|−wldρ⁡(Kn)≥(n−1)−(n−2)=1.|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|-\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\geq(n-1)-(n-2)=1.

Now suppose that n≥8n\geq 8 is even. By Section 3.3.4, wldρ⁡(Kn)≤n−3\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\leq n-3. Therefore,

|Wgreedy|−wldρ⁡(Kn)≥(n−1)−(n−3)=2.∎|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|-\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\geq(n-1)-(n-3)=2.\qed

4 Complete Bipartite Graphs

As in the previous section, we focus primarily on equitable 22-colorings and minimum proper colorings. Throughout, VmV_{m} and VnV_{n} denote the parts of Km,nK_{m,n}, with |Vm|=m|V_{m}|=m and |Vn|=n|V_{n}|=n, and we write Kx,0K_{x,0} and K0,xK_{0,x} for a subset of xx isolated vertices of VmV_{m} and VnV_{n}, respectively. First, we make an observation about subgraphs of complete bipartite graphs.

{lemma}

Let GG be a spanning subgraph of Km,nK_{m,n}, and define

VA={v∈Vm:dG​(v)≥1}andVB={v∈Vn:dG​(v)≥1}.V_{A}=\{v\in V_{m}:d_{G}(v)\geq 1\}\quad\text{and}\quad V_{B}=\{v\in V_{n}:d_{G}(v)\geq 1\}.

Let A=|VA|A=|V_{A}| and B=|VB|B=|V_{B}|. Then |E⁡(G)|≤A⁡(B−κ∗​(G)+1)|E(G)|\leq A(B-\kappa^{*}(G)+1).

Proof.

Let (a1,b1),…,(aκ∗​(G),bκ∗​(G))(a_{1},b_{1}),\dots,(a_{\kappa^{*}(G)},b_{\kappa^{*}(G)}) be the bipartition sizes of each nontrivial component of GG where aia_{i} is the number of vertices belonging to VAV_{A} and bib_{i} is the number of vertices belonging to VBV_{B}. Since the nontrivial components partition VA∪VBV_{A}\cup V_{B}, we have

∑i=1κ∗​(G)ai=A and ∑i=1κ∗​(G)bi=B.\sum_{i=1}^{\kappa^{*}(G)}a_{i}=A\quad\text{ and }\quad\sum_{i=1}^{\kappa^{*}(G)}b_{i}=B.

Note that |E⁡(G)|≤∑i=1κ∗​(G)ai​bi|E(G)|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{\kappa^{*}(G)}a_{i}b_{i}. Since every edge of GG has an endpoint in VnV_{n}, each nontrivial component of GG contains at least one vertex of VBV_{B}. For all i∈[κ∗​(G)]i\in[\kappa^{*}(G)], we then have that bi≤B−(κ∗​(G)−1)=B−κ∗​(G)+1b_{i}\leq B-(\kappa^{*}(G)-1)=B-\kappa^{*}(G)+1 and so

|E⁡(G)|≤∑i=1κ∗​(G)ai​bi≤(B−κ∗​(G)+1)​∑i=1κ∗​(G)ai=A⁡(B−κ∗​(G)+1).∎|E(G)|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{\kappa^{*}(G)}a_{i}b_{i}\leq(B-\kappa^{*}(G)+1)\sum_{i=1}^{\kappa^{*}(G)}a_{i}=A(B-\kappa^{*}(G)+1).\qed

4.1 Equitable 22-Colorings

An equitable 22-coloring of Km,nK_{m,n} has two color classes containing ⌊m​n/2⌋\lfloor mn/2\rfloor and ⌈m​n/2⌉\lceil mn/2\rceil edges. We obtain a sharp upper bound on wld⁡(Km,n)\wld(K_{m,n}) for such a coloring by considering the possible structures of disconnected color classes. We first construct a family of equitable 22-colorings ε2∗\varepsilon_{2^{*}} (see Fig. 4.1).

{construction}

Let 2≤m≤n2\leq m\leq n. We construct an equitable 22-coloring ε2∗\varepsilon_{2^{*}} such that every color class has ⌊n/2⌋+1\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1 connected components.

For even nn, partition the vertices of VnV_{n} into two sets of size n/2n/2. Color all edges incident to the first set with c1c_{1} and all edges incident to the second set with c2c_{2}. Each color class therefore induces a copy of Km,n/2K_{m,n/2}. In each color, the remaining n/2n/2 vertices in VnV_{n} are isolated while the vertices incident to edges of each color form a single nontrivial component. Thus, each color class has n/2+1n/2+1 connected components.

For odd nn, partition the vertices of VnV_{n} into two sets of size ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor and one remaining vertex. Color all edges incident to the first set with c1c_{1} and all edges incident to the second set with c2c_{2}. For the remaining vertex in VnV_{n}, partition the edges equitably between c1c_{1} and c2c_{2}. Consequently, the color classes contain ⌊m​n/2⌋\lfloor mn/2\rfloor and ⌈m​n/2⌉\lceil mn/2\rceil edges, respectively. In each color, the remaining ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor vertices in VnV_{n} are isolated while the vertices incident to edges of each color form a single nontrivial component. Thus, each color class has ⌊n/2⌋+1\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1 connected components.

From (2), for either parity of nn, we have

wldε2∗⁡(Km,n)=2​(⌊n/2⌋+1)−2=2​⌊n/2⌋.\wld_{\varepsilon_{2^{*}}}(K_{m,n})=2\Big(\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1\Big)-2=2\lfloor n/2\rfloor.
4.1.

For any equitable 22-coloring of the edges of Km,nK_{m,n} with 2≤m≤n2\leq m\leq n,

wld⁡(Km,n)≤2​⌊n/2⌋.\wld(K_{m,n})\leq 2\lfloor n/2\rfloor.

Moreover, this bound is sharp.

Proof.

Let G=Km,nG=K_{m,n} with an equitable 22-coloring. We will prove that ∑i=12(κ⁡(Gi)−1)≤2​⌊n/2⌋\sum_{i=1}^{2}(\kappa(G_{i})-1)\leq 2\lfloor n/2\rfloor.

If G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} are connected, then ∑i=12(κ⁡(Gi)−1)=0≤2​⌊n/2⌋\sum_{i=1}^{2}(\kappa(G_{i})-1)=0\leq 2\lfloor n/2\rfloor. We now consider cases where at least one of {G1,G2}\{G_{1},G_{2}\} is disconnected. Since |E⁡(G1)|∈{⌊m​n/2⌋,⌈m​n/2⌉}|E(G_{1})|\in\{\lfloor mn/2\rfloor,\lceil mn/2\rceil\}, we then have

where the second to last inequality follows from the fact that 2​(m​n−1)≥m\sqrt{2(mn-1)}\geq m when nn is even and 2​(m​n−1)≥m+1\sqrt{2(mn-1)}\geq m+1 when nn is odd for 2≤m≤n2\leq m\leq n.

Thus, κ⁡(G1)≤κ⁡(G1′)≤2​⌊n/2⌋+1\kappa(G_{1})\leq\kappa(G_{1}^{\prime})\leq 2\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1, so ∑i=12(κ⁡(Gi)−1)≤2​⌊n/2⌋\sum_{i=1}^{2}(\kappa(G_{i})-1)\leq 2\lfloor n/2\rfloor. By symmetry, if either G1G_{1} or G2G_{2} satisfies the conditions of Section 4.1, we are done.

Case 2. Ai=mA_{i}=m or Bi=nB_{i}=n for each ii. Suppose that Ai=mA_{i}=m. Then

κ⁡(Gi)=κ∗​(Gi)+n−Bi.\kappa(G_{i})=\kappa^{*}(G_{i})+n-B_{i}. (4)

⌊m​n/2⌋\displaystyle\lfloor mn/2\rfloor ≤m⁡(Bi−κ∗​(Gi)+1)\displaystyle\leq m(B_{i}-\kappa^{*}(G_{i})+1)

Combining (4) and (5), we have

κ⁡(Gi)=κ∗​(Gi)+n−Bi≤Bi+1−1m​⌊m​n/2⌋+n−Bi=n+1−1m​⌊m​n/2⌋={n+1−n/2if ​m​n​ evenn+1−n/2+1/(2​m)if ​m​n​ odd\kappa(G_{i})=\kappa^{*}(G_{i})+n-B_{i}\leq B_{i}+1-\frac{1}{m}\lfloor mn/2\rfloor+n-B_{i}=n+1-\frac{1}{m}\lfloor mn/2\rfloor=\begin{cases}n+1-n/2&\text{if }mn\text{ even}\\ n+1-n/2+1/(2m)&\text{if }mn\text{ odd}\end{cases}

For either parity of m​nmn, since m≥2m\geq 2 and κ⁡(Gi)\kappa(G_{i}) is an integer, we have

κ⁡(Gi)≤⌊n/2⌋+1\kappa(G_{i})\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1

Now, suppose that Bi=nB_{i}=n. A similar argument produces

κ⁡(Gi)≤⌊m/2⌋+1≤⌊n/2⌋+1\kappa(G_{i})\leq\lfloor m/2\rfloor+1\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1

Thus, for i=1,2i=1,2, we have κ⁡(Gi)≤⌊n/2⌋+1\kappa(G_{i})\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1 so ∑i=12(κ⁡(Gi)−1)≤2​⌊n/2⌋\sum_{i=1}^{2}(\kappa(G_{i})-1)\leq 2\lfloor n/2\rfloor, and we are done.

In all cases, we have ∑i=12(κ⁡(Gi)−1)≤2​⌊n/2⌋\sum_{i=1}^{2}(\kappa(G_{i})-1)\leq 2\lfloor n/2\rfloor. By Section 2,

wld⁡(G)≤2​⌊n/2⌋.\wld(G)\leq 2\lfloor n/2\rfloor.

The sharpness of the bound is guaranteed by Section 4.1. ∎

4.2 Minimum Proper Colorings

By König’s edge-coloring theorem [6], the complete bipartite graph Km,nK_{m,n} satisfies

χ′​(Km,n)=Δ⁡(Km,n).\chi^{\prime}(K_{m,n})=\Delta(K_{m,n}).

For m≤nm\leq n, every minimum proper coloring of Km,nK_{m,n} uses exactly nn colors. Moreover, each color class is a matching of size mm. For a color cic_{i}, we write MiM_{i} for its monochromatic matching. We determine the wild number for minimum proper colorings of Km,nK_{m,n} and show that it is independent of the choice of proper edge coloring.

4.2.

Let Km,nK_{m,n} be a complete bipartite graph with 2≤m≤n2\leq m\leq n. For any minimum proper coloring ρ\rho of Km,nK_{m,n},

wldρ⁡(Km,n)=n.\wld_{\rho}(K_{m,n})=n.
Proof.

Let M1,…,MnM_{1},\ldots,M_{n} denote the color classes of Km,nK_{m,n} with respect to ρ\rho. Each MiM_{i} consists of mm independent edges, forming mm components of size 2. The remaining n−mn-m vertices are isolated, forming n−mn-m components of size 1. Thus, each color class has m+(n−m)=nm+(n-m)=n components. From Section 2, it follows that

wldρ⁡(Km,n)≥⌈∑i=1n(κ⁡(Mi)−1)n−1⌉=n⁡(n−1)n−1=n.\wld_{\rho}(K_{m,n})\geq\left\lceil\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\kappa(M_{i})-1)}{n-1}\right\rceil=\frac{n(n-1)}{n-1}=n.

To prove the upper bound, take some v∈Vmv\in V_{m} and let WW consist of every edge incident to vv. Note that |W|=n|W|=n.

Consider any color class MiM_{i}. Since MiM_{i} is a matching of size mm, MiM_{i} covers VmV_{m}. Thus, MiM_{i} contains exactly one edge incident to vv. The remaining n−1n-1 edges of WW connect vv to every vertex in VnV_{n} that is not matched to vv in MiM_{i}, including all n−mn-m vertices of VnV_{n} isolated in MiM_{i}. The vertex of VnV_{n} matched to vv in MiM_{i} is already connected to vv by its edge in MiM_{i}.

For any other vertex v′∈Vm∖{v}v^{\prime}\in V_{m}\setminus\{v\}, MiM_{i} matches v′v^{\prime} with some vertex u′∈Vnu^{\prime}\in V_{n}. Thus, the edge u′​v′u^{\prime}v^{\prime} is in MiM_{i}, while the edge u′​vu^{\prime}v belongs to WW. Hence, u′u^{\prime} and v′v^{\prime} are connected to vv in Mi∪WM_{i}\cup W. Therefore, every vertex of Km,nK_{m,n} belongs to the same component of Mi∪WM_{i}\cup W. Since MiM_{i} was arbitrary, WW is color-connecting. Together with the lower bound, WW is ideal and

wldρ⁡(Km,n)=n.∎\wld_{\rho}(K_{m,n})=n.\qed

5 Cartesian Products

Throughout this section, we write ρ\rho for an arbitrary minimum proper coloring of G​□​HG\Box H using χ′​(G​□​H)\chi^{\prime}(G\Box H) colors. Recall that |V⁡(G​□​H)|=|V⁡(G)|​|V⁡(H)||V(G\Box H)|=|V(G)||V(H)| and |E⁡(G​□​H)|=|E⁡(G)||V⁡(H)|+|V⁡(G)|​|E⁡(H)||E(G\Box H)|=|E(G)||V(H)|+|V(G)||E(H)|.

{definition}

Fix minimum proper colorings ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} of GG and HH, respectively, with disjoint color sets. We define ρ∗\rho^{*} as the edge coloring of G​□​HG\Box H where ρ∗​((g,h)​(g′,h))=ρ1​(g​g′)\rho^{*}((g,h)(g^{\prime},h))=\rho_{1}(gg^{\prime}) and ρ∗​((g,h)​(g,h′))=ρ2​(h​h′)\rho^{*}((g,h)(g,h^{\prime}))=\rho_{2}(hh^{\prime}). This coloring is proper and uses χ′​(G)+χ′​(H)\chi^{\prime}(G)+\chi^{\prime}(H) colors, but, in general, is not minimum.

{lemma}

For a minimum proper coloring of G​□​HG\Box H, there exists a color cic_{i} such that (G​□​H)i(G\Box H)_{i} has at least

|V⁡(G​□​H)|−|E⁡(G​□​H)|χ′​(G​□​H)|V(G\Box H)|-\frac{|E(G\Box H)|}{\chi^{\prime}(G\Box H)}

connected components.

Proof.

Let c1,…,cχ′​(G​□​H)c_{1},\dots,c_{\chi^{\prime}(G\Box H)} be the colors of the minimum proper coloring and let mim_{i} be the number of edges colored cic_{i}. Each color class is a matching, so κ⁡((G​□​H)i)=mi+(|V⁡(G​□​H)|−2​mi)=|V⁡(G​□​H)|−mi\kappa((G\Box H)_{i})=m_{i}+(|V(G\Box H)|-2m_{i})=|V(G\Box H)|-m_{i} where

∑i=1χ′​(G​□​H)mi=|E⁡(G​□​H)|.\sum_{i=1}^{\chi^{\prime}(G\Box H)}m_{i}=|E(G\Box H)|.

By averaging, there exists some color cic_{i} such that mi≤|E⁡(G​□​H)|/χ′​(G​□​H)m_{i}\leq|E(G\Box H)|/\chi^{\prime}(G\Box H). Therefore,

κ⁡((G​□​H)i)≥|V⁡(G​□​H)|−|E⁡(G​□​H)|χ′​(G​□​H).∎\kappa((G\Box H)_{i})\geq|V(G\Box H)|-\frac{|E(G\Box H)|}{\chi^{\prime}(G\Box H)}.\qed

The bounds in this section are obtained by bounding from below the number of components of some color class. For an ℓ\ell-edge-colored graph (G,γ)(G,\gamma), we write

clbγ⁡(G)=max1≤i≤ℓ⁡(κ⁡(Gi)−1).\clb_{\gamma}(G)=\max_{1\leq i\leq\ell}(\kappa(G_{i})-1).

Note that clbγ⁡(G)≤wldγ⁡(G)\clb_{\gamma}(G)\leq\wld_{\gamma}(G) by Section 2.

{proposition}

Let n,m≥4n,m\geq 4. Let ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} be any minimum proper colorings of KnK_{n} and KmK_{m}, respectively. Then, for ρ′∈{ρ,ρ∗}\rho^{\prime}\in\{\rho,\rho^{*}\},

wldρ1⁡(Kn)+wldρ2⁡(Km)<wldρ′⁡(Kn​□​Km).\wld_{\rho_{1}}(K_{n})+\wld_{\rho_{2}}(K_{m})<\wld_{\rho^{\prime}}(K_{n}\Box K_{m}).

We consider the cases ρ′=ρ\rho^{\prime}=\rho and ρ′=ρ∗\rho^{\prime}=\rho^{*}. By definition, wldρ1⁡(Kn)≤n−1\wld_{\rho_{1}}(K_{n})\leq n-1 and wldρ2⁡(Km)≤m−1\wld_{\rho_{2}}(K_{m})\leq m-1.

Case 1. ρ′=ρ\rho^{\prime}=\rho. We show that clbρ′⁡(Kn​□​Km)>wldρ1⁡(Kn)+wldρ2⁡(Km).\clb_{\rho^{\prime}}(K_{n}\Box K_{m})>\wld_{\rho_{1}}(K_{n})+\wld_{\rho_{2}}(K_{m}). By Section 5, there exists a color whose corresponding subgraph has at least

components. Since Δ⁡(Kn​□​Km)=n+m−2\Delta(K_{n}\Box K_{m})=n+m-2, we have χ′​(Kn​□​Km)≥n+m−2\chi^{\prime}(K_{n}\Box K_{m})\geq n+m-2. Combining Section 5 with the definition of clbγ⁡(G)\clb_{\gamma}(G), we then have

n​m2−1=n​m−(n2)​m+(m2)​nn+m−2−1\displaystyle\frac{nm}{2}-1=nm-\frac{\binom{n}{2}m+\binom{m}{2}n}{n+m-2}-1 ≤n​m−(n2)​m+(m2)​nχ′​(Kn​□​Km)−1≤clbρ′⁡(Kn​□​Km).\displaystyle\leq nm-\frac{\binom{n}{2}m+\binom{m}{2}n}{\chi^{\prime}(K_{n}\Box K_{m})}-1\leq\clb_{\rho^{\prime}}(K_{n}\Box K_{m}).

Observe that n+m−2<n​m/2−1n+m-2<nm/2-1 since n,m≥4n,m\geq 4, thus

wldρ1⁡(Kn)+wldρ2⁡(Km)≤n+m−2<n​m2−1≤clbρ′⁡(Kn​□​Km)≤wldρ′⁡(Kn​□​Km).\wld_{\rho_{1}}(K_{n})+\wld_{\rho_{2}}(K_{m})\leq n+m-2<\frac{nm}{2}-1\leq\clb_{\rho^{\prime}}(K_{n}\Box K_{m})\leq\wld_{\rho^{\prime}}(K_{n}\Box K_{m}).

Case 2. ρ′=ρ∗\rho^{\prime}=\rho^{*}. Again, we show that clbρ′⁡(Kn​□​Km)>wldρ1⁡(Kn)+wldρ2⁡(Km)\clb_{\rho^{\prime}}(K_{n}\Box K_{m})>\wld_{\rho_{1}}(K_{n})+\wld_{\rho_{2}}(K_{m}). Recall that when nn is even each color class of KnK_{n} is a perfect matching of size n/2n/2 and when nn is odd each color class of KnK_{n} is a near-perfect matching of size (n−1)/2(n-1)/2. Thus, when nn is even the subgraph corresponding to each color class of KnK_{n} contains n/2n/2 components and when nn is odd the subgraph corresponding to each color class of KnK_{n} contains (n+1)/2(n+1)/2 components. Under ρ∗\rho^{*}, the subgraph associated with a color class from ρ1\rho_{1} occurs in each of the mm copies of KnK_{n}, so when nn is even clbρ′⁡(Kn​□​Km)≥n​m/2−1\clb_{\rho^{\prime}}(K_{n}\Box K_{m})\geq nm/2-1 and when nn is odd clbρ′⁡(Kn​□​Km)≥m⁡(n+1)/2−1\clb_{\rho^{\prime}}(K_{n}\Box K_{m})\geq m(n+1)/2-1. Observe that n+m−2<n​m/2−1n+m-2<nm/2-1 and n+m−2<m⁡(n+1)/2−1n+m-2<m(n+1)/2-1 since n,m≥4n,m\geq 4. For either parity of nn, we then have

wldρ1⁡(Kn)+wldρ2⁡(Km)<clbρ′⁡(Kn​□​Km)≤wldρ′⁡(Kn​□​Km).∎\wld_{\rho_{1}}(K_{n})+\wld_{\rho_{2}}(K_{m})<\clb_{\rho^{\prime}}(K_{n}\Box K_{m})\leq\wld_{\rho^{\prime}}(K_{n}\Box K_{m}).\qed

5.2 Complete Bipartite Graphs

{proposition}

Let 2≤m≤n2\leq m\leq n and 2≤s≤t2\leq s\leq t. Let ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} be any minimum proper colorings of Km,nK_{m,n} and Ks,tK_{s,t}, respectively. Then, for ρ′∈{ρ,ρ∗}\rho^{\prime}\in\{\rho,\rho^{*}\},

so it is enough to show that s​n2+m​t2−n−t=n⁡(s​n−1)+t⁡(m​t−1)>0sn^{2}+mt^{2}-n-t=n(sn-1)+t(mt-1)>0 which is true for m,n,s,t≥2m,n,s,t\geq 2. It follows that

wldρ1⁡(Km,n)⋅wldρ2⁡(Ks,t)<clbρ′⁡(Km,n​□​Ks,t)≤wldρ′⁡(Km,n​□​Ks,t).\wld_{\rho_{1}}(K_{m,n})\cdot\wld_{\rho_{2}}(K_{s,t})<\clb_{\rho^{\prime}}(K_{m,n}\Box K_{s,t})\leq\wld_{\rho^{\prime}}(K_{m,n}\Box K_{s,t}).

Thus,

where the first inequality follows from the fact that n​s>1ns>1 for n,s≥2n,s\geq 2.

∎

6 Concluding Remarks

Theorem 3.5 shows that the wild number for KnK_{n} with a minimum proper coloring is exactly the lower bound for 3≤n≤123\leq n\leq 12. These results lead to the following conjecture. {conjecture} For every n≥3n\geq 3 and every minimum proper coloring ρ\rho of KnK_{n},

wldρ⁡(Kn)=⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋.\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})=\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor.

Question 7.5 of [2] asks how far the greedy algorithm can deviate from the wild number. For a minimum proper coloring ρ\rho of KnK_{n}, we showed in Section 3.3.5 that the greedy output is always a forest and therefore has at most n−1n-1 edges. Combining this with Theorem 3.4 gives

0≤|Wgreedy|−wldρ⁡(Kn)≤n−1−⌊4​⌈n/2⌉3⌋.0\leq|W_{\mathrm{greedy}}|-\wld_{\rho}(K_{n})\leq n-1-\left\lfloor\frac{4\lceil n/2\rceil}{3}\right\rfloor.

If the algorithm saturates a color class, then its output is a spanning tree and therefore has exactly n−1n-1 edges. By Section 3.3.5, this output is not ideal whenever n≥7n\geq 7, since smaller color-connecting sets exist by Theorems 3.6 and 3.3.4.
